The app normally reads the MTA's feeds through a small server of its own. Here it replays the 200 alerts it recorded on 12 October 2026, from 10:42 to 14:56 New York time, and the clock stands at the end of that afternoon. Close this window, then interact with it:

  • Click a station or a line to see its alerts, its facts and its art.
  • Drag the timeline handles to wind the clock back and see what arrived when.
  • Zoom with the buttons or the mouse wheel, and drag the map to move it.

0:00 · Turn 1

It started with one spoken paragraph

I've heard that the New York transit authority publishes live updates about closures and similar events. I'd like an HTML page … that draws a map of the New York subway with the stations on it, periodically fetches the updates … and shows those events live on the map. … Keep the history so I can rewind the clock back and forward to the present moment.Pasha, lightly trimmed

Before writing anything, Claude checked what the MTA actually offers:

  • The alerts feed is free and needs no key. One address returns every published alert as plain JSON.
  • The map can be drawn from the MTA's own schedule. It contains the real track geometry and every station's position.
  • History needs a server. A page alone forgets everything when closed, so a small Python program does the fetching and saves what changes.

Everything went into a folder of its own, apart from the Cyber Kitchen episodes.

0:04 · Turn 1

First, we built the page and its server

The first version had all its parts in place:

  • A page with a map area, a list for alerts and a timeline along the bottom.
  • A small server that asks the MTA for its alerts every 30 seconds and saves what changes.
  • A map file built from the MTA's own schedule: every line and every station.

On its first run the server could not reach the MTA, because this Mac's Python had no list of trusted certificates, and the map area came out empty. We fixed both a few minutes later, keeping certificate checks switched on.

0:05 · Turn 1

Five minutes in, we had a live, zoomable map

With the fixes in, everything we had built showed up at once:

  • A zoomable map: all 29 routes and 496 stations in their real positions. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom.
  • Live alerts: stations named in an alert get a coloured ring; an alert for a whole line lights the line.
  • An alert list on the right, showing what is in effect.
  • A timeline along the bottom, with a mark at each change and a Live button.

The feed carried 189 alerts, of which 8 were in effect. Most are planned work for later dates.

0:05 · Turn 1

We built a history you can rewind

The server does not keep a copy of every fetch. It keeps what changed: which alerts arrived and which were removed. The page replays those changes up to any moment, so the slider can take the map back in time.

With only a few minutes of real history, we tested it by placing one invented alert ten minutes in the past, in the browser only, and stepping back to it.

The map showed that one alert and "11 min ago". A reload cleared it.

0:11 – 0:16 · Turns 2 – 4

We worked out what the data can tell us

Before building further, we downloaded the MTA's train feeds and decoded them to see what they hold.

QuestionAnswerWhat the live feeds showed
Which station has the problem?PartlyPlanned work lists its stations. Delays usually name only the line; the place is in the sentence.
Where is each train?Yes, by station164 trains on the numbered lines in one sample, each "stopped at" or "in transit to" a station. No GPS.
When will it arrive?YesPredicted times for up to 20 stops ahead per train.
How fast are things moving?Not directlyNo speed field. It can be worked out from time between stations.

Train history cannot be downloaded later, because the MTA publishes only the present moment. So we started recording straight away, before drawing any of it.

0:16 – 0:22 · Turns 4 – 5

We built a recorder for everything the MTA publishes

One folder per feed under data/, each update a file named by its time.

FolderWhatHow often
alerts/The change log the page replaysChecked every 30 seconds
trains/Positions and predicted arrivals, all eight feeds, exactly as receivedEvery 15 minutes, about 13 MB a day
elevator-…/Elevator and escalator outagesEvery 30 seconds, saved when changed
art/, stations/, paths/ and 18 moreThe MTA's slow-changing datasets and the schedule, 220 MBOn demand

We set trains to every 15 minutes to keep the recordings small, and left out two ridership datasets of 46 and 83 million rows.

0:24 · Turn 5

We added station art, as a carousel

The MTA's Permanent Art Catalog lists 309 artworks in subway stations. We put them on the map.

  • Matching: the catalog names stations in words, so we matched each artwork by name and line. Five needed matching by hand.
  • Carousel: ‹ and › step through a station's artworks. Times Sq-42 St has seven.
  • Text and a link: the catalog has no picture files, only a link to each artwork's page on mta.info, so the card shows the description and that link.
0:26 – 0:29 · Turns 5 – 6

We moved the details into a panel on the right

As there was more to show about each station, we gave it a proper home: a panel that slides in and out, with two tabs.

  • Events: the list of alerts.
  • Selection: everything about what you clicked. For a station: its name and lines, its alerts, facts about it, and its art.
  • One selection at a time: click a station on the map or an event in the list, and the map and the panel follow.
0:30 – 0:33 · Turns 6 – 8

We worked on colour, and made lines selectable

  • Stations take their line's colour, with a thin, soft outline, and are large enough to click easily.
  • Lines can be selected, from the map or from the line circles on a station. The panel shows the line's alerts, the MTA's description and its stations.
  • The page refreshes itself when a file changes, so each change could be seen the moment it was made.

Lines are easiest to click after zooming in, when the stations no longer cover them.

0:37 · Turn 11

We repaired the art catalog's garbled text

Dimitri GerakarisÃ•s Woodside Continuum … Ã’The challenge and opportunity of the Woodside station is in its relationship to the past and to the future,Ã“As the MTA's file has it

253 of the catalog's 394 entries arrive like this. The text was written in the old Mac character set, then misread twice on its way to publication, so one apostrophe arrives as two unrelated characters.

We added a step that reverses both misreadings:

Dimitri Gerakaris’s Woodside Continuum … “The challenge and opportunity of the Woodside station is in its relationship to the past and to the future,”After the repair

95 characters had already been lost at the source, so for those we put back an apostrophe or quotation mark by position, which is a guess. The downloaded file is kept exactly as published.

0:44 – 0:53 · Turns 12 – 19

We built up the timeline in three steps

0:58 – 1:12 · Turns 22 – 30

We tuned how a line with an alert stands out

A line with an alert, or the line you selected, has a soft outline that pulses in a lighter shade of the line's own colour. We got there in steps:

  1. Moving dashes along the line. They ran one way, which suggested a direction the data does not have, so we took the movement out.
  2. A pulsing outline in the alert's colour, such as orange around a blue line.
  3. The line itself brightening, first with a glow, then slightly wider at the peak, then brightness only.
  4. An outline again, in a lighter shade of the line's own colour, a third of the way to white. This is the one we kept.

Along the way we fixed a real fault: every 5-second refresh was redrawing the pulsing shapes, which restarted each pulse and made the map jitter. They are now redrawn only when something changes.

1:14 · Finished

What we ended up with: events

With the Events tab open you can see what is happening and when it started.

  • Top bar: Live, zoom in, zoom out, fit to view, show or hide the panel.
  • Timeline: two handles and clickable marks. Pull them to choose a range, or click a mark to see what arrived then.
  • List: the events that arrived in that range, with a count below.
  • Legend: what each ring colour means.
  • Map: lines with an alert pulse in a lighter shade of their own colour.
1:14 · Finished

What we ended up with: selection

0:00 – 1:19 · The whole conversation

What it took in tokens

Counted from the session's own log, up to the moment this slide was added: 37.1 million tokens across 155 requests to the model, all Claude Opus 5.5.

KindTokensWhat it is
Re-read from cache36,649,630The conversation so far, read again on every request. This is 98.7% of the total and is billed at a small fraction of the normal rate.
New input311,320Text entering the conversation for the first time: Pavel's messages, tool results, files and screenshots.
Output185,116Everything Claude wrote: answers, code, commands and its working notes.
Total37,146,066

The total is large because of how a long conversation works, not because much was written. Each of the 155 requests re-reads everything before it, so the same text is counted again and again: on average about 236,000 tokens of history per request. Not included: the requests made after this count.

What that would cost in dollars

About $13.50 on Claude Opus 5.5, the model that ran the session. The same token counts priced on other models:

ModelRough costNotes
Claude Opus 5.5about $13.50What we used: $7.33 for cache re-reads, $2.49 for new input, $3.70 for output.
Claude Sonnet 5.5about $10.40Its cache-read price is the same as Opus, so the saving is small.
Gemini 3.1 Proabout $19Most requests were over 200,000 tokens, where Gemini doubles its rates.
Gemini 3.8 Flashabout $4At its price through December 2026; it doubles in January 2027.

Caching is what keeps this small. With no caching, every re-read would be billed as fresh input: about $152 on Opus 5.5 and about $138 on Gemini 3.1 Pro.

  • A pricing comparison, not a prediction. Gemini counts tokens differently, and another model would take a different number of steps to do the same work.
  • Two assumptions: cache writes priced at the one-hour rate, twice the input price; and Gemini's hourly charge for keeping a cache alive estimated at 236,000 tokens for 1.3 hours.
  • Prices as of October 2026: Claude from the reference bundled with the app, Gemini from Google's pricing page.
Open

What is not done

  • Trains are recorded but not drawn. Positions and predicted arrivals have been saved every 15 minutes since 0:16. Putting them on the map, on the same timeline, is the obvious next step.
  • Direction. Lines run both ways and the map does not show which way an alert applies. Set aside on purpose.
  • Speed. It has to be worked out from the recordings and the station-to-station distances, which are downloaded but unused.
  • Art has no pictures, and the matching of 309 artworks to stations was spot-checked, not fully checked.
  • No tests. Features first; tests come when Pavel opens a test phase.
  • History has gaps whenever the server is not running.

The conversation that built the app, with Pavel's words as spoken, is in TRANSCRIPT.md.

Not decided

Potential upcoming episodes

Episode 1 looked at the subway from the outside: what is there and what is happening. Two more viewpoints have been talked about. Neither is settled.

EpisodeViewpointWhat it could doWhat it would need
2The riderTrains on the map. Pick home and work, then see the best route right now, the next trains, when to leave, and which alerts or elevator outages are in the way.The recorded train feeds decoded and read live, and a route finder over the schedule.
3The operatorWhat someone at the MTA could learn from the data: where and when things go wrong, how long incidents last, how many riders they touch, and where to put people. Or a live desk for responding to incidents as they arrive.Weeks of recorded history, and invented staffing numbers, since none are published.
